title: Pushes and pulls: the forces around us, and how we feel them

summary.text: You cannot see a force, but you can feel one. Every push and every pull is a force. Forces come from hands and feet, the wind, water, magnets and the Earth. Your child hunts for forces at home, finds who or what gives each one, and sorts big forces from small ones. Then, with eyes shut, they test whether their hand can feel a small packet of rice slipped into a bag. The packet is easy to feel in an empty bag, but easy to miss in a heavy one.
summary.art: A girl with her eyes shut holding a cloth bag by its handles, while a grown-up quietly lowers a small hanky bundle of rice into the bag.

intro.hook: Hold out your hand, palm up, and shut your eyes. Is anything pushing or pulling on your hand right now?
intro.text: Most children say no. But the Earth is pulling your hand down, and your arm is holding it up. Forces are around us all the time, even when we don't notice them. A force is any push or any pull. You can't see a force. You can see what it does, and you can feel it. In this unit you hunt for forces at home. Then you test how well your hand can feel a small one.
intro.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes shut and one open palm held out, with a soft dotted arrow drawn downwards from the palm.

outcomes: By the end I can say that every push and every pull is a force.
By the end I can name things that give forces around me: people and other animals, the wind, water, magnets and the Earth.
By the end I can say that we cannot see a force, but we can see what it does and feel it.
By the end I can tell a big force from a small force by what it does.
By the end I can test, with my eyes shut, whether my hand feels a small extra pull, and count my right answers.
By the end I can explain why a small extra pull is easy to feel in a light bag and hard to feel in a heavy one.

terms.meaning: A force is any push or any pull.
terms.example: A kick, the wind on a kite and the Earth pulling a mango down are all forces.
terms.art: Three small pictures in a row: a foot kicking a ball, a kite in the wind, a mango falling from a tree.

terms.meaning: A push is a force that moves a thing away from the pusher.
terms.example: The wind from a fan pushes a paper away across the table.
terms.art: A table fan blowing a sheet of paper off the edge of a table.

terms.meaning: A pull is a force that moves a thing towards the puller.
terms.example: A fridge magnet pulls a steel pin towards itself.
terms.art: A fridge magnet with a steel safety pin jumping towards it.

terms.meaning: Gravity is the pull of the Earth. It pulls everything down towards the ground.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a dropped spoon to the floor, and pulls a full bag down on your fingers.
terms.art: A steel spoon falling from a child's hand towards a tiled floor.

terms.meaning: A big force does a big job, like lifting a full bucket. A small force does a small job, like lifting a feather.
terms.example: Pulling a full bucket up from a well needs a big pull. Picking up a tissue needs only a small pull.
terms.art: A woman pulling a heavy bucket up from a well beside a child lifting a tissue with two fingers.

terms.meaning: A nerve is a thin thread in your body that carries messages. Nerves in your skin send news of every push and pull to your brain.
terms.example: When a bag pulls on your fingers, nerves in your fingers send that news to your brain.
terms.art: A simple drawing of a hand with thin lines running from the fingertips up the arm.

terms.meaning: A balance compares two weights. Its two pans hang level when both sides pull down the same.
terms.example: A vegetable seller puts weights on one pan and tomatoes on the other until the pans are level.
terms.art: A two-pan market balance with brass weights on one pan and red tomatoes on the other, hanging level.

explanations.concept: Every push and every pull is a force
explanations.definition: A force is any push or any pull. Every force is between two things: one gives the push or pull, and the other is pushed or pulled.
explanations.description: In the force hunt, you found pushes and pulls all over the home. Your hand pulled a drawer open. The wind from the fan pushed a paper. The Earth pulled a falling spoon to the floor. A magnet pulled a paper clip. Scientists give them all one name: force. For every force, ask two questions. Who or what gives the force? And who or what gets pushed or pulled?
examples: In the force hunt, the tap water pushed a steel cup in the sink.
A crow pulls a twig from a broom to build her nest.
At the Rath Yatra in Puri, in Odisha, thousands of people pull huge wooden chariots with ropes.
explanations.art: A home drawn as a cut-away doll's house, with small labelled pictures of a hand opening a drawer, a fan blowing a paper and a spoon falling.

explanations.concept: We cannot see a force, but we see and feel what it does
explanations.definition: A force cannot be seen. We know a force is there because we see what it does, or because we feel it on our body.
explanations.description: Nobody has ever seen the wind's push itself. We see the clothes flap on the line, and we feel the wind on our face. Nobody has seen the Earth's pull. We see a mango fall, and we feel a full bag pull on our fingers. A force can start a thing moving, stop it, or squash it. It can also press on you while nothing moves. In the Secret Packet test, the bag hung still, and you still felt it pulling your hand down.
examples: In the Secret Packet test, the still bag pulled down on your fingers.
A fridge magnet holds a paper up, and the paper does not fall.
During the monsoon in Kerala, strong winds bend the coconut trees.
explanations.art: Clothes flapping on a washing line on a flat's balcony, with wavy lines showing the wind.

explanations.concept: Forces can be big or small
explanations.definition: Some forces are big and some are small. A bigger force does a bigger job: it lifts a heavier thing, or pulls a thing down harder.
explanations.description: In the Secret Packet test, the bag with two water bottles pulled hard on your fingers. The empty bag hardly pulled at all. Both pulls were forces, one big and one small. You can tell a big force from a small one by what it does. A big pull bends your fingers and makes your arm tired. You hardly notice a small pull. A rubber band stretches a lot for a big pull and only a little for a small one.
examples: In the Secret Packet test, the bag with two bottles pulled much harder than the empty bag.
Lifting a full pressure cooker needs a bigger pull than lifting a steel spoon.
A breeze pushes a feather. A storm can push over a tree.
explanations.art: Two hands side by side: one holding a light cloth bag easily, one bent down by a bag with two big water bottles.

explanations.concept: How your hand feels a pull
explanations.definition: Your skin, muscles and joints have tiny sensors that notice pushes and pulls. Your hand notices a change in a pull by comparing it with what it already holds.
explanations.description: When a bag pulls on your fingers, your skin is pressed and stretched. Tiny sensors in your skin notice this. Nerves then send the news up your arm to your brain. In the Secret Packet test, the packet pulled down by the same amount both times. In the empty bag, the packet was a big part of the whole pull, so you felt it. In the heavy bag, it was a tiny part, so you often missed it.
examples: In the Secret Packet test, the packet is usually easy to feel in the empty bag.
In the Secret Packet test, with the heavy bag you may get only about half your answers right. That is what guessing gives.
You notice your school bag when you first put it on. After a while, you stop noticing it.

perspectives.explanation: The nerves in your hand carry signals, like wires. The feeling of 'heavy', and the comparing, happen in the brain.

Sensing happens all along the way. The nerve cells in your skin notice the pull themselves, and they send fewer signals when a pull stays the same for a while. Your body as a whole feels the bag, not only your brain.

explanations.art: A close-up drawing of a fingertip with a hanky bundle pressing on it, and tiny dots in the skin lighting up.

agreed.text: Every push and every pull is a force.
agreed.evidence: Scientists use the one word force for a kick, the wind on a sail, water pushing a boat, a magnet pulling a pin and the Earth pulling a mango down.

agreed.text: Forces cannot be seen. We know them by what they do and by how they feel.
agreed.evidence: Nobody has seen the Earth's pull, but every dropped thing falls, and every held bag pulls on the hand.

agreed.text: The smallest extra weight a person can notice grows with the weight they already hold.
agreed.evidence: Ernst Weber showed this in Germany in the 1830s, by asking people to compare weights. Many tests since then have found the same.

challenging.claim: If nothing is moving, there are no forces.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A still room looks as if nothing is happening.
challenging.against: The Earth pulls the tumbler on the table all the time, and the table pushes it up. The still bag in the Secret Packet test pulled on your fingers the whole time.
challenging.context: This card is about whether forces are there when nothing moves.

challenging.claim: A careful hand can feel any extra weight, however small.
challenging.for: In the Secret Packet test, the packet was easy to feel in the empty bag. So it seems that paying attention is enough.
challenging.against: In the Secret Packet test, the same packet was often missed in the heavy bag, however hard the child tried. Ernst Weber found the same in the 1830s: the heavier the load, the bigger the extra weight must be before a person notices it.
challenging.context: This card is about how well our hands feel weight.

challenging.claim: The wind is not a force, because you cannot see the wind.
challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: We see a hand push a door, but we never see the air doing anything.
challenging.against: No force can be seen, not even a hand's push. We see what the wind does: kites rise, clothes flap and boats with sails move. That is how we know the wind pushes.
challenging.context: This card is about forces we cannot see.

challenging.claim: Only beings with a brain can sense a push.
challenging.for: We feel a push through our nerves and brain, and so do other animals like dogs and crows.
challenging.against: A touch-me-not plant has no brain, yet she senses a finger's touch and folds her leaves within seconds. So a plant can sense a touch without a brain. Some scientists say this is an automatic response, not a feeling.
challenging.context: This card is about who can sense pushes and pulls.

big_questions.q: Why can a balance notice a small extra pull that a hand misses?
big_questions.hint: A balance compares two sides side by side. What does a hand compare the packet with?

big_questions.q: Could there be a force so small that nothing at all could notice it?
big_questions.hint: In the Secret Packet test, your hand missed the packet in the heavy bag, but a balance noticed it. Could something notice even smaller forces than a balance?

big_questions.q: Is heaviness in the bag, or in your hand?
big_questions.hint: In the Secret Packet test, the packet was the same in the empty bag and in the heavy bag. What changed was what your hand already held.

big_questions.q: You and a friend hold the same bag. You say it is heavy, and your friend says it is light. Who is right?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each of you was holding before, and how strong each of your arms is.

story.title: The Lemon in the Bag
story.note: Two-pan balances are still used at some vegetable markets in India, though many sellers now use electronic scales. Ammamma means grandmother in Telugu. Sravani, Kiran, Ammamma and Lakshmamma are made up.
text: Sravani was seven. She lived in Secunderabad, a busy city next to Hyderabad.
Every Sunday, she went to the vegetable market with her grandmother, Ammamma. Her little brother Kiran came too. He was five.
Ammamma always gave Sravani the small cloth bag. 'You are in charge of the curry leaves and the coriander,' she said.

The market was full of pushes and pulls. A man pushed a cart of onions through the crowd. A goat pulled at a bunch of spinach until the seller shooed her away. The wind from a big fan made the plastic sheets flap over the stalls.
At the tomato stall, Lakshmamma the seller used a two-pan balance. She put a brass weight on one pan and tomatoes on the other. The pans swung up and down. Then they stopped, hanging level.
Sravani held her little bag of leaves. It hardly felt like anything at all.
Then she felt a tug. Her bag pulled down on her fingers, just a little more than before. She looked inside. A lemon sat on top of the curry leaves.
'Who put this here?' she asked.
Kiran giggled behind Ammamma's sari. 'I did! I wanted to see if you would feel it.'
'Of course I felt it,' said Sravani. 'My hands feel everything.'
Next, Ammamma bought potatoes, a pumpkin and a packet of rice. They all went into the big jute bag.
'Hold this for me while I pay,' Ammamma said. 'Your arms are strong now.'
The big bag pulled hard on Sravani's hands. She held the handles tight and stood very still.
Kiran tiptoed up behind her. Very gently, he slipped another lemon into the big bag.
'Did you feel it?' he asked.
'Feel what?' said Sravani.
Kiran pointed. A lemon sat on top of the potatoes.
Sravani frowned. 'That's not fair. I felt the lemon in the little bag. Why didn't I feel this one?'
'Was it a bigger lemon, or a smaller one?' asked Ammamma.
'The same kind,' said Sravani. 'Just as small as the first one.'
'Then let us ask Lakshmamma's balance,' said Ammamma.

Lakshmamma laughed. She took the lemon out and hung the big bag on one side of her balance. She added weights to the other pan until the two sides were level. Then she dropped the lemon back into the bag.
Down went the bag's side, at once.
'The balance felt it,' said Kiran. 'And you didn't!'
On the way home, Sravani was quiet. She was thinking.
The lemon pulled down just as much in both bags. In the little bag, the lemon was a big part of what she held. In the big bag, the lemon was only a tiny part.
'I know!' she said. 'My hand noticed the lemon when it was big next to what I was holding. In the heavy bag, it was too small to notice.'
At home, she gave Kiran an empty steel tiffin box. 'Shut your eyes,' she said. She dropped in three coins. Kiran felt them at once.
Then she filled the tiffin box with rice. She gave it back to him. Very gently, she laid three coins on top.
Kiran opened his eyes. 'Did you put them in yet?'
'They're already there,' said Sravani, and she showed him.
'So my hands are bad at feeling,' said Kiran sadly.
'No,' said Sravani. 'Your hands are good at feeling changes. A change is easy to feel when you are holding very little.'
Ammamma smiled. 'That is why Lakshmamma uses a balance,' she said. 'Her hands hold heavy bags all day. The balance is fair to everyone.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: Sravani finds that the same lemon was easy to feel in a light bag and went unnoticed in a heavy one, though it pulled down just as much both times. Her hand noticed a change by comparing it with what it already held. The balance showed the lemon every time.
ask: Kiran put a lemon in the little bag. Did Sravani feel it? How did she know?
Why did Sravani not notice the lemon in the big bag?
How did the balance show that the lemon was there?
Was Kiran right that his hands are bad at feeling? What did Sravani tell him?
art: A busy vegetable market with a man pushing an onion cart, a goat tugging at spinach and plastic sheets flapping.
A girl holding a small cloth bag, peering in at a lemon on top of curry leaves, while her little brother giggles behind their grandmother.
A seller with a two-pan balance, the jute bag on one side dipping down as a lemon drops in.
At home, a girl laying coins on a steel tiffin box full of rice while her brother holds it with his eyes shut.

experiments.title: The Secret Packet: can your hand feel a small extra pull?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hold a cloth bag with your eyes shut. A grown-up sometimes slips a small packet of rice into it. You say whether you felt it. First the bag is empty. Then it holds two full water bottles.
experiments.question: Can your hand feel a small packet of rice slipped into an empty bag? Can it feel the same packet slipped into a heavy bag?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you feel the packet in the empty bag? Will you feel it in the heavy bag? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same packet, the same bag and the same hand every time. Your eyes stay shut, so you can only feel, not see. A coin toss decides when the packet goes in, so you cannot guess a pattern. We try six times with each bag, because one right answer could be a lucky guess.
results_table: My guess: will I feel it?

materials.item: a light cloth shopping bag with handles
two full 1-litre water bottles, with their caps on
a hanky with 2 big spoons of rice tied up in it (the secret packet)
paper and a pencil, for the tally

schedule.what: Guess, then do six tries with the empty bag and six with the heavy bag, and count the right answers.

experiments.record: Draw the two bags. Under each, draw a tick for every right answer and a cross for every wrong one. Count the ticks.

setup.art: A hanky with a small heap of rice in the middle, its corners tied into a knot to make a soft bundle.
setup.caption: 1. Tie 2 big spoons of rice in a hanky. This is the secret packet.

setup.art: A girl sitting on a chair with her eyes shut, holding an empty cloth bag by its handles, her arm bent at the elbow.
setup.caption: 2. Shut your eyes. Hold the empty bag still.

setup.art: A grown-up tossing a coin, then gently lowering the hanky bundle into the bag the girl is holding.
setup.caption: 3. Toss a coin. Heads: the packet goes in. Tails: it does not.

setup.art: The same girl, eyes shut, holding the bag now with two big water bottles inside, and a tally sheet with ticks and crosses on the table.
setup.caption: 4. Do it again with two bottles in the bag. Count the ticks.

flow.do: 1. Tie 2 big spoons of rice in a hanky. 2. Let your child hold the empty bag, then the bag with two bottles. 3. Let them feel the packet in their hand.
flow.say: This is our secret packet. Hold the empty bag. Now hold it with two bottles in it. Which bag pulls your hand down more?
flow.kid: Hold the empty bag. Now hold the heavy bag. Which pulls more?

ask.q: Which bag pulls your hand down more?
good: The heavy one pulls my fingers down a lot.

flow.parent: Your child should sit with the arm bent at the elbow and the bag hanging just above their lap. That way the arm does not get tired.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason for each bag. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: You will shut your eyes. Sometimes I will slip the packet in. Will you feel it in the empty bag? In the heavy bag? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will you feel the packet in the empty bag? In the heavy bag? Why?

good: I will feel it both times, because I can feel things in my hand.
Maybe not in the heavy bag, because it already pulls a lot.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes and holds the empty bag. 2. Toss the coin quietly. 3. Heads: lower the packet gently into the bag. Tails: put your hand in, but take it out empty. 4. Ask 'In or not in?' 5. Mark a tick or a cross. 6. Take the packet out. Do six tries.
flow.say: Eyes shut. Hold the bag still. Now tell me: did the packet go in, or not?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Hold still. Did the packet go in? Say 'in' or 'not in'.
flow.parent: Put your hand into the bag every time, so the movement is the same. Lower the packet slowly until it rests, and don't drop it. A fan running in the room hides any small sounds.

flow.do: 1. Put the two full bottles in the bag. 2. Do six more tries, exactly as before. 3. Mark a tick or a cross each time. 4. Count the ticks for each bag.
flow.say: Now the heavy bag. Eyes shut again. Did the packet go in, or not?
flow.kid: Now the heavy bag. Eyes shut. Did the packet go in?

ask.q: Was it easier or harder this time?
good: I was just guessing with the heavy bag.

flow.parent: Results differ from child to child. Often the packet is felt 5 or 6 times out of 6 in the empty bag, and only about 3 times in the heavy bag, which is no better than guessing. If your child gets nearly all the heavy-bag tries right, use a smaller packet of 1 spoon of rice and try again. If they miss it in the empty bag too, use 4 spoons of rice. Let your child rest their arm between tries. Whatever your child finds is a real result.

flow.do: Count the ticks together. Ask your child what they found, and why. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: How many did you get right with the empty bag? With the heavy bag? The packet was the same both times. Why do you think it was harder to feel in the heavy bag?
flow.kid: Count your ticks for each bag. Which bag was harder? Why?

ask.q: Why was the packet harder to feel in the heavy bag?
good: The bag was already pulling a lot, so a little more did not feel different.
The packet was tiny next to the bottles.

flow.parent: First let your child say what they found and why. Then say it plainly: the packet pulled down just as much both times. In the empty bag it was a big part of the pull, so the hand felt it. In the heavy bag it was a tiny part, so the hand missed it.

check.q: You hold a bag with two bottles in it, with your eyes shut. A packet is slipped in and you cannot tell it is there. Was the packet still pulling the bag down?
options: Yes, just as much as in the empty bag
Only a little, because the bag was full
check.why: The Earth pulls the packet down by the same amount wherever it is. The pull was there. Your hand missed it because the bag was already pulling hard.

experiments.title: Push the Scale: how big is your push?
experiments.context: In this experiment you push down on a bathroom scale with one finger, one hand and two hands. The scale shows how big each push is as a number. You can do this only if your home has a bathroom scale.
experiments.question: Which push is biggest: one finger, one hand or two hands? Do two hands push twice as hard as one hand?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which push will show the biggest number? Will two hands show twice as much as one hand? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same scale on the same floor every time. You kneel in the same place and push straight down. You hold each push steady for three seconds before we read the number, so the number can settle.

materials.item: a bathroom weighing scale, digital or with a dial (if your home has one)

schedule.what: Guess, push the scale with a finger, one hand and two hands, and write down each number.

experiments.record: Write the number for each push. Draw a tall bar for a big number and a short bar for a small one.

setup.art: A bathroom scale on a tiled floor, and a boy kneeling in front of it pressing down with one finger.
setup.caption: 1. Kneel. Push down with one finger. Hold it steady.

setup.art: The same boy pressing down on the scale with both palms, arms straight, while a grown-up reads the number.
setup.caption: 2. Now push with one hand, then with two hands. Read each number.

flow.do: 1. Put the scale on a hard, flat floor. 2. Show how the number goes to zero with nothing on it. 3. Ask for guesses and reasons.
flow.say: This scale shows how hard something pushes on it. Which push will show the biggest number? Will two hands show twice as much as one hand? Why?
flow.kid: Which push will be biggest? Will two hands show twice as much as one hand? Why?
flow.parent: Put the scale on a dry, flat, non-slip floor, and hold its edge with your foot so it does not slide. A digital scale may need a tap with your foot to switch on. Some will not show a number for a very small push. If the finger push shows zero, that is a result too. If the scale shows nothing at all, skip this experiment.

flow.do: 1. Your child kneels and pushes down with one finger as hard as they can, for three seconds. 2. Read the number. 3. Then one hand. 4. Then two hands. 5. Write each number.
flow.say: Push with one finger, as hard as you can. Hold it. What does it say? Now one hand. Now two hands.
flow.kid: Push with one finger. Hold it. Read the number. Now one hand. Now two hands.

good: Two hands showed the biggest number.

flow.parent: The scale shows kilograms. It is really measuring the push on it, and showing that as if it were a weight.

flow.do: Compare the numbers. Ask whether two hands gave twice as much as one hand. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at the numbers. Did two hands show twice as much as one hand? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Did two hands show twice as much as one hand? Why?

ask.q: Why might two hands not be twice as much?
good: I can only push as hard as my body can lean.

flow.parent: Two hands usually give a bigger number than one hand. Whether it is twice as much depends on how much of their body weight your child leans onto their hands.

check.q: You push a scale with one finger, then with your whole hand. Which shows the bigger number?
check.why: A whole hand can give a bigger push than one finger, so the scale shows a bigger number.

activities.title: Who Is Pushing? A force hunt at home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and find pushes and pulls. For each one, you say who or what gives the force: a person, another animal, the wind, water, a magnet or the Earth.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with two columns: 'People and other animals' and 'Other givers'
a fridge magnet and a steel paper clip, if you have them

schedule.what: Hunt for 8 forces at home and sort them by who gives them.

activities.record: Draw each force in its column. Count how many are in each column.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns headed 'People and other animals' and 'Other givers', and small drawings starting to fill each one.
setup.caption: 1. Make a two-column sheet.

setup.art: A girl in a kitchen turning on a tap so the water pushes a steel cup, while she draws it on her sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Find a force. Who or what gives it? Draw it in the right column.

flow.do: Show the two columns: one for forces given by people and other animals, and one for forces given by other things. Do one example together: drop a steel spoon on a mat.
flow.say: Every push and every pull is a force. Watch the spoon fall. Something pulled it down. Who gave that pull?
flow.kid: Watch the spoon fall. What pulled it down?
flow.parent: If your child says 'nothing', ask why the spoon went down and not up. Then say: the Earth pulls everything down. Scientists call that pull gravity.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home together. 2. Find at least 8 forces. 3. For each one, ask: who or what gives the force? 4. Your child draws it in a column.
flow.say: Let's find forces. Turn on the tap. Hold a paper near the fan. Put the magnet near the paper clip. Who or what is pushing or pulling each time?
flow.kid: Find a push or a pull. Who or what gave it? Draw it.

ask.q: Who gave the push when the fan blew the paper?

flow.parent: Good ones to try: tap water pushing a cup, the fan's wind pushing a paper, a magnet pulling a paper clip, the Earth pulling a dropped ball, an ant pulling a crumb, and you pulling a drawer. Keep fingers away from the fan blades.

flow.do: Count each column. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many forces did people and other animals give? How many did other things give? Which column has more?
flow.kid: Count each column. Which has more?

check.q: Water from a tap pushes a paper boat along the sink. Who gives the push?
check.why: The water pushes the boat. A force always has a giver, even when it is not a person.

activities.title: Eyes Shut: push or pull on your hand?
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up gently pushes or pulls your hand while your eyes are shut. You say whether it was a push or a pull, and whether it was big or small. It shows that you can feel a force without seeing anything.

materials.item: nothing to buy: just a grown-up and a child

schedule.what: Feel pushes and pulls on your hand with your eyes shut, and name each one.

activities.record: Draw your hand. Add one arrow for a push you felt and one arrow for a pull you felt.

setup.art: A girl with her eyes shut and her hand held out flat, and a grown-up gently pressing her palm with two fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Shut your eyes. Hold out your hand.

setup.art: The grown-up gently tugging the girl's fingers towards themself, while the girl says 'pull'.
setup.caption: 2. Say: push or pull? Big or small?

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes and holds out one hand. 2. Gently push the palm, or gently pull the fingers. 3. Mix big and small. 4. After each one, your child says push or pull, big or small.
flow.say: Eyes shut. I am going to push or pull your hand. Tell me which one, and if it was big or small.
flow.kid: Eyes shut. Push or pull? Big or small?

ask.q: How did you know it was a pull?
good: I felt my fingers being tugged.

flow.parent: Keep every push and pull gentle. Try a very light touch with one fingertip too. Can your child still feel it?

flow.do: Swap: your child pushes and pulls your hand while your eyes are shut. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Now you push or pull my hand, and I will guess. Could you see the force, or only feel it?
flow.kid: Now you push or pull. I will guess. Can we see a force?

check.q: With your eyes shut, how did you know a force was on your hand?
check.why: Your eyes were shut, so you could not see anything. Your skin felt the push or pull. We know forces by what they do and by how they feel.

activities.title: Kitchen Forces: make panakam and name every push and pull
activities.context: In this activity you make panakam, a cool drink of jaggery, water and lemon from South India. As you make it, you name every push and pull you use.

materials.item: jaggery, about 2 big spoons, grated or broken small
a jug of water, about 2 tumblers
a pinch of cardamom powder or dry ginger powder, if you have it
a steel spoon, a knife and a lemon squeezer, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the lemon with the knife.

schedule.what: Make panakam together and count the pushes and pulls.

activities.record: Draw three kitchen forces you used. Write 'push' or 'pull' next to each.

setup.art: A boy squeezing half a lemon over a steel jug of brown jaggery water, with a grown-up holding the jug.
setup.caption: 1. Squeeze the lemon. That is a push.

setup.art: The boy stirring the jug with a steel spoon, and a tally of pushes and pulls on a paper beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Stir, pour and count every force.

flow.do: 1. Pull open the drawer for the spoon. 2. Pour the water into the jug. 3. Add the jaggery and stir. 4. Cut the lemon (grown-up). 5. Your child squeezes it. 6. Add the cardamom and stir again.
flow.say: Every time you push or pull, say it out loud. Opening the drawer: push or pull? Pouring water: who pulls the water down?
flow.kid: Say each push or pull out loud. Who pulls the water down?

ask.q: When you pour water, what pulls it down into the jug?

flow.parent: Squeezing the lemon is a push from your fingers. Stirring is pushes in a circle. Pouring is the Earth pulling the water down. Opening the drawer is a pull.

flow.do: Count the pushes and pulls you named. Drink the panakam. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many forces did we use to make one drink? Which was the biggest force?
flow.kid: Count your forces. Which was biggest?

check.q: Your fingers squeeze a lemon to get the juice out. Is that a push or a pull?
check.why: Your fingers press into the lemon. That press is a push, and every push is a force.

games.title: Force Bingo: who gave the push or pull?
games.players: 2 players, a parent and a child. With 3 or 4 players, two can share a board as a team.
games.context: This is a bingo game. One player reads a caller card about a push or a pull. Everyone finds who or what gave the force on their own bingo board.

items.f: The Earth
An ant

img.credit: Jake Nitta, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: A bullock

img.credit: Paul Asman, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: The Earth
A crow
A mango falls from the tree.
A kite flies up high at Uttarayan.
A steel pin jumps across the table to a magnet.
A ball flies across the room after a kick.
A paper boat rushes along a rain gutter.
A grain of rice moves slowly across the floor.
A soap bubble floats away from your lips.
A rubber band is stretched back with a paper ball in it. Then it is let go, and the ball flies.
A cart of sugarcane rolls down the village road.
A fishing boat bobs up and down near the beach.
A twig is lifted onto a branch for a nest.
A clothes clip snaps shut on a towel.

rules: Each player takes one bingo board, or a team shares one. Take 9 small paper scraps each to cover squares. The boards are 3 rows of 3 squares.
Mix the 12 caller cards. Players take turns reading the top card out loud, front side only.
Everyone says who or what gave the force. The reader turns the card over to check the answer.
If that giver is on your board, cover it. If it is not, do nothing.
The first player to cover a full row, up, down or across, calls 'Force!' and wins. If two players finish on the same card, they both win.
If nobody has a row after all 12 cards, the player with the most squares covered wins.

setup.art: Two printed bingo boards with nine squares each, with the words The wind, The Earth, A magnet and An ant written in the squares.
setup.caption: 1. Each player takes a board.

setup.art: A child reading a caller card out loud while another child covers 'The wind' on her board with a scrap of paper.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Cover the giver.

flow.do: Hand out the boards and paper scraps. Read the rules together.
flow.say: One of us reads what happened. We both say who or what gave the force. Then we cover it on our boards.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Who gave the force? Cover it.

flow.do: Play. After some cards, ask whether the force was a push or a pull.
flow.say: A mango falls from the tree. Who gave the force? Was it a push or a pull?
flow.kid: Who gave the force? Push or pull?

ask.q: Was the Earth's force on the mango a push or a pull?
good: A pull. It pulled the mango down.

flow.parent: Some cards can be argued either way, such as the ant moving a grain of rice. Accept a push or a pull if your child can say why. The stretched rubber band pushes the paper ball forward as it springs back. The clothes clip is a spring pushing the two sides together. Accept a good reason over a quick answer.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is one last card to try.
flow.kid: Answer one last card.

check.q: A dry leaf blows across the balcony floor. Who gave the push?
check.why: The wind pushes the leaf. We can't see the wind, but we can see what it does.

games.title: The Force Caller: move the way the force moves you
games.players: 2 or more players. One reads the cards and the others move. With 2 players, a parent and a child, you swap roles.
games.context: This is a moving game. The reader names a force, and the movers move as if that force were pushing or pulling them. When the reader says 'Still!', everyone freezes.

items.f: A strong wind pushes you from behind.
items.b: Big force. Lean and step forward.

items.f: Pretend you are a steel pin. A giant magnet on the wall pulls you.
items.b: Big force. Slide towards the wall.

items.f: The Earth pulls you extra hard.
items.b: Big force. Sink down slowly to the floor.

items.f: A big wave pushes you towards the beach.
items.b: Big force. Rock forward and back.

items.f: A rope ties you to a friend, who pulls gently.
items.b: Small force. Walk slowly towards the puller.

items.f: A soft breeze pushes a feather in your hand.
items.b: Small force. Move one hand gently.

items.f: A rubber band pulls your arm back.
items.b: Small force. Pull one arm back a little.

items.f: A crowd pushes you on a busy train platform.
items.b: Big force. Take small steps sideways.

items.f: You hold a heavy bag of rice.
items.b: Big force. Bend one arm down low.

items.f: Still! No new force.

rules: Mix the 10 force cards. The reader reads the front of one card out loud, then the back, which says whether the force is big or small and how to move.
Everyone else moves the way that force would move them. Big forces mean big moves, and small forces mean small moves.
On the 'Still!' card, everyone freezes. Anyone who moves becomes the next reader.
The game ends when all 10 cards have been read.

setup.art: A caller holding up a card while two children lean forward as if pushed by a strong wind.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a force.

setup.art: Two children frozen like statues mid-move, one with an arm reaching towards a wall.
setup.caption: 2. Move the way it moves you. Freeze on 'Still!'.

flow.do: Clear a space. Read the rules.
flow.say: I will name a force. Move the way it would move you. A big force means a big move.
flow.kid: Listen to the force. Move like it moves you.

flow.do: Play all 10 cards. After two or three cards, ask what gave the force.
flow.say: A strong wind pushes you from behind. Move! Who gave that push? Was it big or small?
flow.kid: Move with the force. Who gave it? Big or small?

ask.q: Which card was the smallest force?
good: The feather one, because I hardly moved.

flow.parent: This game lets your child feel that every force has a giver, a direction and a size.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is one question about the game.
flow.kid: Answer one question.

check.q: In the Force Caller game, which card has the biggest force?
options: A big wave pushes you towards the beach
A soft breeze pushes a feather
check.why: A big wave can push a whole person. A breeze on a feather is a small force, and 'Still!' adds no new force.

projects.title: My Force Diary: three days, three forces a day
projects.context: In this project you keep a diary for three days. Each day you draw three forces you noticed, say who or what gave each one, and mark it big or small.

materials.item: a notebook or 3 sheets of paper

schedule.what: Draw three forces you noticed at home today. Write who gave each one.
Draw three forces you noticed outside, on the way somewhere or from the window.
Draw three forces you could feel but not see. Look back at all nine, and count the big and small ones.

projects.record: Nine drawings, each with the giver's name and a B for big or an S for small.

setup.art: An open notebook page with three boxes: a drawing of a bucket being pulled up, a kite in the wind and a dropped ball.
setup.caption: 1. Each day, draw three forces.

setup.art: The same notebook with a big B or a small S written next to each drawing.
setup.caption: 2. Write who gave each force, and B for big or S for small.

flow.do: Day 1: help your child choose three forces from the home and draw them.
flow.say: What three pushes or pulls did you see today? Who gave each one? Was it big or small?
flow.kid: Draw three forces from today. Who gave each one?

flow.do: Day 2: look for forces from a window or on a walk. Your child draws three more.
flow.say: Look outside. Can you find a force that a person did not give?
flow.kid: Look outside. Draw three forces. Can you find one not made by a person?

ask.q: Which force did a person not give?
good: The Earth pulling the rain down.

flow.do: Day 3: your child draws three forces they can feel but not see. Then look at all nine drawings and count the big forces and the small ones.
flow.say: Draw three forces you can feel but not see, like your school bag pulling on your shoulders. Now count the big ones and the small ones.
flow.kid: Draw three forces you can feel. Count the big ones and the small ones.

check.q: Your school bag pulls on your shoulders. Who gives that pull?
options: The Earth, pulling the bag down
check.why: The Earth pulls the bag down, and the bag's straps pull on your shoulders. You feel the pull, though you cannot see it.

challenges.title: Catch the Secret Packet: build a hanger balance
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Secret Packet test, your hand often missed the packet in the heavy bag. Can you build something that shows when the packet goes in?
challenges.problem: In the Secret Packet test, your hand could not tell when the rice packet went into the heavy bag. Build something that shows it every time, without using your hand to feel.
constraints: You may not look inside the bag to check.
It must work for an empty bag first. Then try it with heavy bags.
materials: two plastic carry bags of the same kind, or two paper cups of the same kind with string
a door handle or a curtain rod to hang it from
the secret packet from the Secret Packet test
a pencil and paper to mark where the two ends of the hanger rest
general: Vegetable sellers use a two-pan balance: weights on one side, vegetables on the other.
Shops use electronic scales that show the weight as a number.
Doctors weigh babies on a scale, not by holding them.
creative: Hang two bags of the same kind from the ends of a hanger. Mark where the ends rest on a paper behind it.
Hang a single bag from a rubber band, and mark how far it stretches.
Sit the bag on a kitchen sponge and watch whether the sponge squashes a little more.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own packet-catcher. Does it show the packet in an empty bag? Does it still show it when each bag holds a small 500 ml water bottle? Draw your design.

setup.art: A plastic clothes hanger hanging from a door handle, with a plastic carry bag tied to each end, hanging level.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a bag from each end of a hanger. Make it level.

setup.art: The same hanger tipped a little to one side after a hanky bundle of rice is dropped into one bag, with a pencil line on paper behind showing where it was.
setup.caption: 2. Drop in the packet. Does that side go down?

flow.do: Read the problem. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: In the Secret Packet test, your hand missed the packet in the heavy bag. What could you build that shows when the packet goes in?
flow.kid: In the Secret Packet test, your hand missed the packet. What could you build to catch it?

good: A hanger with a bag on each end.
A rubber band that stretches more.

flow.do: 1. Help your child build their idea. 2. For a hanger balance, hang one bag on each end. 3. Move the bags until the hanger hangs level. 4. Mark where the ends are. 5. Drop the packet into one bag. 6. Then put a small 500 ml water bottle in each bag, make it level again, and drop the packet into one bag.
flow.say: Make it hang level first. Now drop in the packet. Did one side go down? Now put a small 500 ml bottle in each bag and try again.
flow.kid: Make it level. Drop in the packet. Did it tip?
flow.parent: Hang the hanger low, from a door handle you can reach, and keep feet clear in case a bottle falls. With empty bags, the hanger tips clearly. With a bottle in each bag, it tips only a little, so watch the pencil marks closely. A small tip still counts. If it does not move at all, that is a real result. A longer stick, such as a broom handle hung from its middle by a string, can tip more.

flow.do: Talk about what worked. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Did your packet-catcher work with empty bags? With heavy bags? How is it like the vegetable seller's balance in the story, The Lemon in the Bag?
flow.kid: Did it catch the packet? With heavy bags too?

check.q: Two bags of the same kind hang level on a hanger. You drop a packet into the left bag. What happens?
check.why: The packet adds a pull on the left side, so the left side goes down. A balance compares the two sides.

items.p: Who gave the force? A grown-up reads each one. Sort them into the two groups.
items: The wind blowing clothes on a line
The Earth pulling a falling leaf
A crow pulling a worm from the soil
A magnet holding a note on the fridge
items.why: Forces come from people and other animals, and also from the wind, water, magnets and the Earth. A strong answer names the giver each time.

items.p: Draw a line from each giver to the thing it moves.
items.why: Each giver gives a push or a pull. The wind pushes the kite, the Earth pulls the mango, the magnet pulls the pin, and your breath pushes the bubble.
items.art: Four givers on the left (wind, Earth, magnet, a child's face blowing) and four pictures on the right (kite, mango, pin, bubble).

items.p: In the Secret Packet test, why do you shut your eyes?
opts: So you cannot see the packet go in
items.why: With your eyes shut, you can only feel. That way the test checks your hand, not your eyes.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: Which bag pulls your hand down more?
opts: The bag with two full water bottles
items.why: The bottles are heavy, so the Earth pulls that bag down harder. A strong answer says the heavy bag gives a bigger pull.

items.p: Draw one force in your home. Draw who or what gives the force, and the thing it moves.
items.a: Any real push or pull, with the giver and the thing moved, such as a hand opening a door or a fan blowing a paper.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both parts of a force: the giver and the thing that is pushed or pulled.

items.p: You can see a force.
items.why: False. We never see a force itself. We see what it does, like a mango falling, and we feel it, like a bag pulling our fingers.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: how do you know the wind is pushing, when you cannot see the wind?
items.a: I can see what the wind does. The clothes flap, the kite goes up and I feel it on my face.
items.why: A strong answer gives evidence: something the wind moves, or something the child feels.

items.p: Every push and every pull is a ____.
items.why: Force is the scientists' word for any push or any pull.

items.p: Meenakshi and her brother Arjun did the Secret Packet test.

views.says: My hand is great at feeling. It felt the packet in the empty bag every time.
Hands are bad at feeling. Mine missed the packet in the heavy bag.

items.ask: Who is right? Say why, and a grown-up can write it down. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: Each is right about one bag. A hand feels a small change easily when it holds little, and misses it when it holds a lot. So a hand feels a change by comparing it with what it already holds.
items.why: A strong answer uses the results from both bags, and does not call either child simply wrong.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: You did the force hunt at home. You found 4 pulls and 5 pushes. How many forces did you find?
items.why: 4 and 5 more make 9. Every push and every pull is a force, so you found 9 forces.

items.p: Three of these are the Earth pulling. Which one is not?
opts: A mango falls from a tree
A kite rises in the wind
A ball rolls down a slope
items.why: The kite rises because the wind pushes it up. The Earth pulls things down, not up.

items.p: A bucket is pulled up a well with a rope. Is the rope's force a push or a pull?
items.why: The rope pulls the bucket up towards the person above. Every pull is a force.

items.p: Put the steps of the Secret Packet test in order.
items: Shut your eyes and hold the empty bag
Put two bottles in the bag and do six more
Count the ticks for each bag
items.why: We guess first, so the test can check the guess. We count at the end to compare the two bags.

items.p: Look at the girl flying a kite. Write the giver next to each arrow.
labels: the arrow pushing the kite up
the arrow pulling the string towards the girl
the arrow pulling the kite towards the ground
items.why: The wind pushes the kite up, the girl pulls the string, and the Earth pulls the kite down. One kite has three forces on it at once.
items.art: A girl on a flat's terrace flying a kite, with three arrows: one up from the wind, one along the string to her hands, and one down from the kite.

items.p: Someone says: 'There are no forces in a still room.' Name two forces that are there right now. Say them out loud, and a grown-up can write them down.
items.a: The Earth is pulling everything down, like the cups on the shelf. The floor is pushing up on the chair. My clothes press on my skin.
items.why: A strong answer names real forces that act while nothing moves, such as the Earth's pull and a shelf or floor holding things up.

items.p: Draw yourself holding a heavy bag. Show where you feel the pull.
items.a: A child holding a bag, with the fingers or shoulder marked where the pull is felt.
items.why: A strong drawing marks the fingers, hand or shoulder, where the bag pulls down.

items.p: A big push and a small push are both forces.
items.why: True. Every push is a force, whatever its size. A breeze on a feather and a storm on a tree are both forces.

items.p: Big force or small force? Sort these jobs.
items: Pulling a full bucket up from a well
items.why: Heavy jobs need big forces and light jobs need small ones. A strong answer thinks about how heavy each thing is.

items.p: You push a bathroom scale with one finger, and it shows 2 kilograms. With one hand, it shows 8 kilograms. What might two hands show?
items.why: Two hands can push harder than one hand, so the number goes up. It may not be quite twice as much.

items.p: Lakshmamma sells tomatoes in a market. Her son Ravi helps her. They talk about holding bags of vegetables.

views.says: I always weigh on my balance. It is fair to everyone.
I can tell how heavy a bag is just by holding it. The balance takes too long.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the Secret Packet test to say why. A grown-up can write it down. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Lakshmamma for heavy bags, because a hand can miss a small extra in a heavy load. It also says Ravi is right that a hand can guess quickly, and can feel small changes in light bags.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test and is fair to both sides.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: Think of the Secret Packet test with just one water bottle in the bag. Would the packet be easier or harder to feel than in the bag with two bottles? Why? Say it out loud, and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: Easier, because the packet is a bigger part of what the hand holds when there is only one bottle.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea that a hand compares a change with what it already holds.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: Your hand missed the packet in the heavy bag. What could help you feel it better?
opts: Lift the bag up and down gently
Hold the bag very, very still
items.why: Lifting helps a little, because your muscles and joints join in. Ernst Weber found that people compare weights better when they lift them.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: Divya touches the leaf of a touch-me-not plant, and the leaves fold up.

views.says: The plant felt my finger's push, so she folded her leaves.
The plant sensed the touch and responded. Some scientists call this an automatic response, not a feeling.

items.ask: What do you think? Give one reason, and a grown-up can write it down. Then say what the other side has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as the leaves folding within seconds of the push. It also notes that both sides agree the plant sensed the push.
items.why: Plants sense pushes and pulls. Whether to call this feeling is still argued about. A strong answer is fair to both sides.

items.p: Draw a way to show the secret packet going into a heavy bag, without using your hand to feel it.
items.a: A balance, a hanger with two bags, a rubber band that stretches more, or a scale.
items.why: A strong drawing shows something that changes when the packet goes in, such as one side of a balance going down.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: If your hand misses a force, the force is not there.
items.why: False. In the heavy bag, the packet still pulled down, and a balance showed it. Our hands miss small changes in big pulls.
items.context: This question is about the Secret Packet test. With your eyes shut, you hold a cloth bag while a grown-up sometimes slips in a small packet of rice. First the bag is empty, then it holds two full water bottles.

items.p: On the space station, the astronaut Sunita Williams holds a bag of rice. What does the bag do?
opts: It floats, and hardly presses on her hand
It pulls her hand down hard
items.why: Inside the space station, everything floats, so the bag does not press on her hand. The Earth still pulls the bag, but the bag and the station fall around the Earth together.

items.p: To compare two weights fairly, a vegetable seller uses a ____.
items.why: A balance shows small differences that a hand would miss in a heavy load.

items.p: Three of these are forces. Which one is not?
items.why: A colour is not a push or a pull, so it is not a force.

items.p: Your Force Diary has 9 drawings. 4 of the forces were big. How many were small?
items.why: 9 take away 4 is 5. So 5 of the forces were small.

items.p: In the Secret Packet test, you feel the packet in the heavy bag on your first try. Does that prove your hand can feel it? What should you do next? Say it out loud, and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: No. One right answer could be a lucky guess. You should try many more times and count how many you get right.
items.why: A strong answer says that one try can be luck, and that more tries show the real pattern.

quiz.p: Which of these is a force?
quiz.why: A kick is a push, and every push is a force. A colour or a name does not push or pull.

quiz.p: A kite goes up on a windy day at the Uttarayan kite festival in Gujarat. What gives the push?
quiz.why: The wind pushes the kite up. If you chose 'nothing', you may think a force must be seen. Look at what the kite does instead.

quiz.p: A mango falls from a tree in Ratnagiri, in Maharashtra. What pulls it down?
quiz.why: The Earth pulls everything down. That pull is called gravity.

quiz.p: A fridge magnet holds a paper up. Can you see the magnet's force?
opts: No, but we see that the paper stays up
Yes, it looks like a thin line
quiz.why: No force can be seen. We know the magnet's force is there because the paper does not fall.

quiz.p: Which job needs the biggest pull?
opts: Pulling a full bucket of water up from a well
Pulling a feather off a pillow
Pulling a tissue from a box
quiz.why: The full bucket is heaviest, so it needs the biggest pull. A strong reason talks about how heavy the thing is.

quiz.p: You shut your eyes and hold an empty cloth bag. A grown-up slips in a small rice packet. What will most likely happen?
quiz.why: The packet is a big part of what you hold, so your hand notices the extra pull.

quiz.p: You shut your eyes and hold a cloth bag with two full water bottles in it. A grown-up slips in a small rice packet. What will most likely happen?
quiz.why: The packet is a tiny part of what you hold, so your hand often misses it. If you chose 'every time', you may think a hand feels any small extra weight.

quiz.p: Which one of these is a pull?
opts: A magnet drawing a steel pin towards itself
A fan blowing a paper away
quiz.why: A magnet moves the pin towards itself, so it pulls. A kick and a fan's wind both push things away.

quiz.p: How can you tell that a force is big?
opts: It does a big job, like lifting something heavy
quiz.why: We cannot see a force. We tell a big one from a small one by what it does.

quiz.p: A child pushes a swing, and a crow pulls a twig from a broom. Which of these is a force?
quiz.why: Every push and every pull is a force, whoever gives it.

applications: Shops weigh rice, dal and vegetables on scales, so every customer gets a fair amount. Hands miss small differences in heavy loads.
Doctors and nurses weigh newborn babies on a scale, not by holding them.
Many lifts have a sensor that feels the push of the people inside, and beeps if there are too many.
Engineers such as Allison Okamura, at Stanford University in the United States, build robot tools for surgeons that let the doctor feel how hard the tool is pushing.

spotted.text: At the Rath Yatra in Puri, in Odisha, thousands of people pull huge wooden chariots with long ropes.
spotted.art: A giant wooden chariot on a street, with crowds pulling on thick ropes.

spotted.text: In the snake boat races in Kerala, long lines of rowers push the water back with their oars, and the boat shoots forward.
spotted.art: A long, narrow snake boat on a green river, with rows of rowers dipping their oars together.

spotted.text: At the Uttarayan kite festival in Gujarat, the wind pushes kites up and the flyers pull on their strings.
spotted.art: Rooftops covered with people flying bright kites in a blue sky.

spotted.text: At Chennai Central railway station, porters carry heavy suitcases on their heads. The Earth pulls the load down, and their necks and backs push up.
spotted.art: A porter in a red shirt carrying a suitcase on his head along a busy platform.

spotted.text: At a vegetable market in Madurai, a seller weighs onions on a two-pan balance.
spotted.art: A woman at a vegetable stall holding up a two-pan balance with onions on one pan and weights on the other.

open_questions.q: How does the brain turn signals from your hand into the feeling of 'heavy'?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know which sensors in the skin, muscles and joints notice a pull. How all these signals come together into one feeling of heaviness is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How does a plant sense the weight of her own fruit and branches?
open_questions.why_open: Plants that are bent or shaken often grow thicker, stronger stems. Scientists are still working out how plant cells sense these pushes and pulls.

open_questions.q: Why does lifting a bag help us compare weights better than holding it still?
open_questions.why_open: Ernst Weber noticed this in the 1830s. Many scientists think our muscles and joints add their own news when we lift. Exactly how the body combines it all is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the Secret Packet test, you got 5 right out of 6 with the empty bag. With the heavy bag, you got 3 right. How many more did you get right with the empty bag?
maths.explain: Count on from 3 to 5: 4, 5. That is 2 more. So the empty bag was easier by 2 right answers.
maths.context: This is about the Secret Packet test, where you held a bag with your eyes shut and said when a rice packet went in.
maths.why_maths: Taking the smaller number from the bigger one shows how much easier the empty bag was.

maths.problem: If you did not feel anything at all and just guessed 'in' or 'not in', about how many of 6 tries would you get right?
maths.explain: Each guess has two choices, and one of them is right. So about half the guesses are right. Half of 6 is 3. If you get only about 3 right with the heavy bag, you were probably guessing.
maths.context: This is about the Secret Packet test, where you said 'in' or 'not in' six times for each bag.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what guessing gives helps you tell whether your hand really felt the packet.

maths.problem: In the force hunt at home, you found 5 forces given by people and 7 forces given by other things, like the wind and the Earth. Make a tally of each. Which group has more, and by how many?
maths.explain: The tally shows 5 marks for people and 7 for other things. 7 is more than 5. 7 take away 5 is 2. So other things gave 2 more forces.
maths.context: This is about the force hunt, where you found forces at home and sorted them by who gave them.
maths.why_maths: A tally lets you compare two groups at a glance.

maths.problem: You pushed a bathroom scale with one hand, and it showed 6 kilograms. With two hands, it showed 10 kilograms. Is 10 double 6?
maths.answer: No. Double 6 is 12, and 10 is 2 less.
maths.explain: Double means two lots of the same. 6 and 6 make 12. Your two hands gave 10, which is less than 12. So two hands gave more than one hand, but not double.
maths.context: This is about Push the Scale, where you pushed a bathroom scale with a finger, one hand and two hands.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows whether two hands really push twice as hard as one.

roots.context: We hunted for forces at home, felt pushes and pulls with our eyes shut, and did the Secret Packet test. Now we ask what the Secret Packet test tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Secret Packet test, with your eyes shut, you felt the packet go into the empty bag. In the bag with two bottles, you often missed the same packet. The packet pulled on your hand just as much both times. So your hand feels a change in a pull by comparing it with what it already holds.
deep_truth.habit: We trust our hands to tell us how heavy things are, the way a scale does. The Secret Packet test shows that a hand judges a change by comparing it with what it already holds.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Secret Packet test, the packet is usually easy to feel in the empty bag. With the heavy bag, results often fall to about half right, which is what guessing gives. A balance can show the packet that the hand misses.

three.who_am_i: You are someone who feels forces. Your skin, nerves and brain notice pushes and pulls on you, and compare them with what came before.
three.what_is_life: Every living being senses pushes and pulls. A touch-me-not plant folds her leaves at a touch, and a spider feels a fly tugging at her web.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of forces we cannot see: the Earth's pull, the wind's push and the floor holding us up.

roots.thread: A kick, the wind, a magnet and the Earth's pull look like very different things. Scientists give them all one name, force, and trace them back to just a few basic forces of nature. Every force is between two things: one gives it, and the other gets it. Feeling a force also takes two: the thing that pushes or pulls, and the body that notices it. One view is that your skin and nerves already notice and compare, before the brain gets the news. Many scientists say instead that feeling happens only in the brain, and that nerves just carry messages.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the senses touch things, they bring cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go, and they do not last. Bear them calmly.
teachings.link: In the Secret Packet test, the same packet was felt in the empty bag and missed in the heavy bag. A feeling depends on both you and the thing, so it changes from one moment to the next.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught that feeling comes from contact. A feeling arises only when there is contact.
teachings.link: In the Secret Packet test, the packet's pull reached your hand only through contact with the bag. Whether you felt it also depended on what your hand already held.

science.text: Weber's law: the smallest extra weight a person can notice grows roughly in step with the weight they already hold. It has been tested many times since the 1830s.
Nobody yet fully knows how the signals from skin, muscles and joints come together into the feeling of heaviness.

other_view.view: The nerves in your hand are like wires. They only carry signals. The feeling of heavy, and the comparing, are work done by the brain.

practice.title: Feel the forces on you
practice.say: Sit still and shut your eyes. Feel the floor or the chair pushing up under you. Feel your hands resting on your knees. Feel how heavy they are. Feel your clothes on your skin. Now hold one hand out, palm up, and feel the Earth pulling it down. Rest it again. Which of these forces had you stopped noticing before we began?
practice.kid: Sit still. Shut your eyes. Feel the floor push up. Feel your hands on your knees. Feel your clothes. Hold one hand out. Feel it pulled down. Which force had you forgotten?

ask: In the Secret Packet test, your hand missed the packet in the heavy bag. Was the packet's pull still there?
Is the heaviness of a bag in the bag, or in your hand?
Which forces on you right now have you stopped noticing?

how_we_found_out.who: Ernst Heinrich Weber, a German doctor and scientist. Later, Gustav Fechner, a German scientist, and Ardem Patapoutian, a scientist born in Lebanon who works in the United States
how_we_found_out.when: The 1830s (Weber's tests), 1860 (Fechner) and 2021 (the Nobel Prize for the touch sensors)
how_we_found_out.story: It seems natural to think that a careful hand can feel any extra weight, however small, if you pay attention. In the 1830s, a doctor named Ernst Weber tested this in Leipzig, in Germany. He asked people to hold two weights and say which was heavier. A small extra was easy to notice when the weight was light. When the weight was heavy, the same small extra was missed. To be noticed, the extra had to grow as the load grew. Weber also found that people did better when they lifted the weights than when the weights just rested on a still hand. In 1860, another German scientist, Gustav Fechner, named this rule Weber's law. Much later, in 2021, Ardem Patapoutian, a scientist born in Lebanon, shared the Nobel Prize for finding the tiny touch sensors in our nerve cells.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People assume a careful hand can feel any small extra weight. Weber showed that the extra must be bigger when the load is heavier, so a small extra in a heavy load goes unnoticed.

G. T. Fechner, Elemente der Psychophysik (1860), where the rule is named after Weber.
B. Coste and others, 'Piezo1 and Piezo2 are essential components of distinct mechanically activated cation channels', Science 330 (2010).
The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2021, shared by David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian for their discoveries of receptors for temperature and touch.

playtest: Walked through every step as a parent and child would in a flat. The Secret Packet test needs only a cloth bag, two water bottles, a hanky of rice and a coin, and a note now says results differ from child to child. The bingo game was played with 2 and with 4 players: the rules now say who reads, who wins and what happens if nobody gets a row. The Force Caller cards now carry big or small, and the magnet card no longer pulls a person's hands. Names are introduced where they first appear, family members were removed from the steps, one duplicate joke, question and counting exercise were swapped for new ones, and the missing hanger-balance step was added.
